issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' as a trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only broad internal-state trigger alongside trauma-linked cues (hearing related names, ambulances) and is weakly connected to the rest of the formulation. The other nodes emphasize intrusive war memories, negative self-appraisals, and avoidance; a relaxation trigger without any corresponding threat content or appraisals about letting guard down is clinically hard to anchor here.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors
issues.explanation: 'Keep checking mirrors' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. Mirror checking usually implies appearance/body-focused concern or hypervigilant scanning for current danger, but this profile has no Threat items and the formulation isolates Threat from the active network. The remaining maladaptive strategies (avoiding sleep, revenge fantasies) fit trauma intrusions and appraisals, whereas mirror checking addresses a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

vignette:
At seventy-seven, Minh Tran had spent most of his adult life in the United States and decades working as a firefighter, yet the scenes that returned to him most forcefully were from much earlier, when he was a civilian boy in a war zone in Southeast Asia. In the first sessions, he spoke about those years carefully, as if approaching something dangerous. He remembered the day with unusual sharpness: the sudden blast that split the air, the concussion of it in his body, the screaming that followed, and the chaos of people running while ambulances arrived too late for some and frantically for others. Certain names were shouted over and over that day—family members, neighbors, the names of men being searched for, the names of the dead—and those sounds seemed to attach themselves to the horror of the moment. Even now, hearing related names spoken in the right tone could stop him cold. What made these recollections unsettling to Minh was not only how detailed they were, but how strange they felt. He would describe the memory as clear enough to see, almost frame by frame, while also insisting that it did not feel like it had happened to him, as though he were carrying around someone else’s story in his head.

In the years after the war, Minh built a life defined by usefulness, discipline, and endurance. He married, raised a family, and entered fire service, a profession whose emergency rhythms were familiar to him in ways he rarely discussed. He did his job well, but even during his working years there were moments when the old terror broke through without warning. The sound of an ambulance approaching the station could pull his attention away from whatever was in front of him. A sudden bang—equipment dropping, a backfire, a distant construction blast—could bring the wartime scene into his mind before he had time to orient himself. These memories did not come when invited. They arrived on their own, vivid and unwelcome. He might be standing in the bay or sitting at home and suddenly be back in that earlier world, hearing the blast and the shouts of names as if they were happening again.

Minh had come to believe that letting himself think directly about what happened was risky. If he started, he feared he would not be able to handle where his mind would go. He did not say this dramatically; it was more like a private rule he had lived by for years. He kept himself moving, alert, occupied. In the firehouse and later in retirement, he scanned his surroundings almost constantly, checking entrances, listening for changes in sound, noting who was nearby and what might go wrong. He experienced this as common sense rather than excess. To him, danger was something a person survived by noticing first. His vigilance had a cost, though. His wife had long noticed that he rarely seemed fully at ease, even in their own home, and that a walk through a parking lot or a crowded waiting room could leave him tense and watchful, his eyes moving from one corner to another.

Sleep became another battleground. Minh delayed going to bed as long as he could. Lying in the dark felt too exposed, too close to the return of images he did not trust himself to bear. Some nights he stayed up until exhaustion overpowered him, sitting in a lit room rather than entering the bedroom. He spoke less about nightmares than about the dread of surrender involved in sleep itself. The darkness and stillness gave too much space for the memory to enter. Over time this habit wore on him physically and narrowed his life with his wife; evenings that might once have been companionable became shaped around his resistance to bedtime and his need to stay on guard.

Alongside this, Minh carried bitter thoughts about the people responsible for the violence he lived through. At times he imagined revenge in detailed, private fantasies that he did not act on and did not want to act on, but that gave form to the anger he had kept tightly contained for years. He also judged himself harshly. Somewhere in him was the conviction that someone else would not have gotten into that situation, would have known what to do, would have been less helpless. When he spoke about the civilians caught up in the attack, he often slipped into language that flattened human experience, including his own. He said that in those moments he had felt like an object, something moved around by forces outside him, not like a person whose life mattered.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was not a single crisis but the growing recognition, in older age, that these experiences were not loosening their grip. Retirement had removed some of the structure that once helped him contain them. Ambulance sirens in the neighborhood, a bang from nearby construction, or hearing a familiar wartime name at a community gathering could still pull him abruptly into the past. He came in because he was tired of organizing his nights around avoiding sleep and tired of living as if every environment needed to be searched for danger. What frightened him most was the possibility that if he let himself look directly at the past, he would come apart. What he hoped, cautiously, was not to forget, but to have the memories feel like his own life at last rather than an alien, invading thing.
